reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a ChatGPT-branded Ethereum arbitrage bot as a beginner-accessible source of passive income, claiming returns of $1,000 or more per day and over 25% per day. It instructs viewers to deploy a smart contract, deposit at least 0.2 ETH into the contract or bot address, and use start and withdrawal controls, while showing a balance rising to 2.541 ETH and reporting further gains. Although it mentions gas or burn fees that could reduce profits, the central message solicits Ethereum deposits based on unusually high passive-return claims.

citations.quote: Today, I'll be walking you through the process of deploying an Ethereum arbitrage bot using ChatGPT which is your ticket to easy daily passive income.
With the smart contract deployed, fund it with some Ethereum, which will be used for trading
So I have about 2.31 Ethereum which is over 15% profit already.
So it basically took me a day to make over 25% of my deposit back!
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address

opening.argument: Judge, the funding guidance should be read alongside the creator's warning that fees can exceed trading gains. The stated minimum is explained as a way to avoid that loss, not as a condition for receiving a fixed payout. The speaker also says profits fluctuate. Those qualifications do not prove the bot works, but they make the presentation a discussion of a risky trading process rather than an unconditional promise of returns.

citations.quote: If you fund the contract with 0.2 ETH or less and the bot targets another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.2 ETH just to make sure that won't happen.
The profits fluctuate week to week?

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies a deposit instruction and striking profit claims, but those claims do not establish a guaranteed return. Its reading of the minimum deposit leaves out the accompanying explanation that fees could consume more than the bot makes. The speaker's account of a profitable day can be questioned without treating every described outcome as a promise to viewers.

citations.quote: the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
So it basically took me a day to make over 25% of my deposit back!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A fee warning does not neutralize the central pitch: the video calls the bot a route to easy daily passive income, then tells viewers to fund it. The claimed gain is presented as the result of running the bot, while the supplied material does not independently establish that trading produced it. Acknowledging possible fees is compatible with using an unusually high return claim to induce deposits.

citations.quote: which is your ticket to easy daily passive income.
With the smart contract deployed, fund it with some Ethereum, which will be used for trading
So it basically took me a day to make over 25% of my deposit back!

opening.argument: Judge, much of the presentation is an operational walkthrough. The speaker describes asking ChatGPT for contract code, placing it in a Remix file, matching the Solidity compiler version, and deploying through a wallet. That sequence gives viewers steps they can inspect and perform; the profit account appears within a demonstration of operating the deployed contract. It is reasonable to classify the video's central activity as teaching a smart-contract workflow without assuming that the reported result is independently verified.

citations.quote: Hey Chat GPT, write me the code for a smart contract on Ethereum to auto-trade the arbitrage opportunities between Uniswap and SushiSwap.
Next copy this code from chatgypt and paste it into the file bot.sol you've just created
under the compiler select the 0.6.6 version so that it matches our contract.
Head over to the deploy and run transactions tab in Remix.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening is right that viewers are told to fund a contract, but funding is also a step in the workflow being demonstrated. The speaker explicitly describes the Ethereum as trading funds. Neither the quoted deposit instruction nor the reported balance change, on its own, establishes that the walkthrough is a transfer to the creator or that the claimed trading result was fabricated.

citations.quote: With the smart contract deployed, fund it with some Ethereum, which will be used for trading
So I have about 2.31 Ethereum which is over 15% profit already.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The programming steps are real parts of the pitch, but they lead directly to instructions to deposit Ethereum and start the bot. The tutorial framing does not remove the promise of easy passive income or verify the reported gains. The video presents deployment as a means to obtain returns, not merely as an exercise in writing and compiling Solidity.

citations.quote: Today, I'll be walking you through the process of deploying an Ethereum arbitrage bot using ChatGPT which is your ticket to easy daily passive income.
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
The last step is to click start, this will enable the bot to start monitoring the market and execute trades.

opening.argument: Judge, the described arrangement is a user-deployed trading tool, not an identified payment to the presenter. The instructions call it the viewer's own bot, direct funding to the viewer's contract address, and describe a withdrawal control that returns funds to the wallet. That account does not prove the contract is safe or that it earns anything. It does, however, leave a crucial mechanism unshown: these sources do not establish that deposits go to an address controlled by the speaker or that the speaker receives the funds.

citations.quote: After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet
You can see the balance from the Bot is now in my wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the funding step as solicitation, but its cited wording says to use the viewer's exact contract address. The speaker also describes withdrawal back to a wallet. The unusually high return claims warrant skepticism; they do not, by themselves, show who controls the contract's funds or that the presenter takes them.

citations.quote: to your exact contract/bot address
withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet
So it basically took me a day to make over 25% of my deposit back!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it the viewer's bot does not establish who ultimately controls funds or what the supplied contract code does. Viewers are directed to obtain that code from a linked source, deploy it, and fund it with at least 0.2 ETH. The withdrawal account and displayed balances do not independently verify the promised trading mechanism or returns. The deposit instructions remain tied to the claim of substantial passive income.

which is your ticket to easy daily passive income.
